family_diagnostics.inflorescence: A head (capitulum) made of many small florets packed onto one receptacle.
family_diagnostics.floret_types: Heads may contain ray florets, disc florets, or both.
family_diagnostics.involucre: One or more series of phyllaries subtend the head and are often critical for identification.
family_diagnostics.fruit: Cypsela, often with a pappus of scales, awns, or bristles.
family_diagnostics.field_tip: To learn Asteraceae well, do not stop at flower color. Look at phyllaries, receptacle/paleae, leaves, pappus, and overall architecture.

visual_lesson.teaching_order: whole plant → high-value structure → reproductive confirmation → exception/tie-breaker
visual_lesson.intro: The fastest upgrade in composite-family ID is realizing the 'flower' is usually a whole inflorescence.

steps.title: 1 · Turn the head sideways
steps.look_for: A head of many florets sitting above a basket of green phyllaries.
steps.why_it_matters: That turns one apparent flower into a capitulum and immediately points toward Asteraceae.

steps.title: 2 · Separate ray from disk
steps.look_for: Each apparent yellow 'petal' is a ray floret; the center contains many disk florets.
steps.why_it_matters: This is the core mental-model shift for the family.

steps.title: 3 · Inspect the underside
steps.look_for: Phyllary number, shape, overlap, hairs and tips around the involucre.
steps.why_it_matters: Phyllaries are often more diagnostic than flower color.

steps.title: 4 · See a family exception
steps.look_for: No daisy rays; separate male and female plants carry discoid heads.

steps.title: 5 · Follow one floret to fruit
steps.look_for: One inferior ovary under one floret becoming a 1-seeded cypsela, often with a pappus.
steps.why_it_matters: This confirms the family after the head architecture gets your attention.

steps.title: 6 · Flip the head over
steps.look_for: Four broad outer phyllaries forming a conspicuous square/collar-like base beneath the yellow head.
steps.why_it_matters: This is the video-fed lesson in why the underside of an Asteraceae head can identify a plant faster than flower color.

comparisons.title: Radiate vs discoid
comparisons.rule: Radiate heads have ray + disk florets. Discoid heads lack rays. Both are fully Asteraceae.

comparisons.title: Ray floret ≠ petal
comparisons.rule: A ray is one whole flower, not one petal of a larger flower.

visual_lesson.caveat: Do not identify the family from a daisy-like outline alone; verify the involucre, individual florets and fruit.

family_confusion_cleanup.field_question: Is this really one flower, or a head made of many florets—and what structure proves Asteraceae rather than a merely daisy-looking family?
look_here_first: Turn the apparent flower sideways/over: find an involucre of phyllaries beneath a common receptacle.
Zoom into the face: prove that the head contains multiple individual florets; a ray is a whole floret, not a petal.
Follow one floret downward: the ovary is inferior and matures as a one-seeded cypsela, commonly carrying a pappus.

comparison_matrix.separate: Asteraceae has true florets packed on a receptacle inside a phyllary involucre; inspect individual florets and fruit/pappus rather than head silhouette.
Apiaceae 'heads' resolve into umbels/umbellets with pedicellate 5-part flowers and schizocarp fruits; Asteraceae resolves into sessile florets on one receptacle with phyllaries and cypselas.
Do not use a round flower cluster alone. Asteraceae confirmation is involucre + multiple florets on one receptacle + inferior one-ovule fruiting units/cypselas.

exception_locks: Rays can be absent: Baccharis and many Eupatorieae are still Asteraceae.
A head can contain only ray-like florets or only disc florets; sunflower shape is not required.
Pappus may be conspicuous, reduced, scale-like, awned, or absent; absence of fluff does not eject a plant from the family.
Phyllary shape/series can be genus- or species-diagnostic, but a green bract under a flower cluster by itself is not enough.
genus_routing_cues: First split head type: radiate vs discoid vs ray-only/ligulate.
Then inspect phyllary series/tips/hairs and whether the receptacle bears paleae.
Then use pappus form, cypsela characters, leaf arrangement and whole inflorescence architecture.
For thistle-like plants inspect phyllaries and pappus; for Eupatorieae-like fluffy heads inspect discoid florets plus opposite/alternate leaves and involucre.
